  • Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized every 4 hours and every 1 hour PRN wheezing/dyspnea

tabs.title: History & Physical
tabs.html: M.L., 30-year-old female. Persistent asthma since childhood. Admitted 3 days ago with a severe asthma exacerbation; required intubation for 20 hours. Chest x-ray on admission: right lower lobe (RLL) infiltrate — community-acquired pneumonia. Extubated on hospital day 2 and transferred to the medical unit yesterday. No tobacco use. No known drug allergies.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for M.L., a 30-year-old client with asthma and right lower lobe pneumonia who was transferred from the ICU yesterday. Refer to the Nurses’ Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which findings in the 0300 assessment require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Restless, repeatedly pulling at the nasal cannula
Speaking 3–4 words at a time
Trachea midline with symmetric chest expansion
Sternocleidomastoid muscles contracting with each breath
Coughing thick yellow sputum
SpO₂ 88% on 2 L/min
optionRationales: Correct. New restlessness is an early sign of hypoxia.
Correct. Speaking only a few words at a time shows severe dyspnea and increased work of breathing.
A midline trachea and symmetric expansion are reassuring and make tension pneumothorax unlikely.
Correct. Accessory muscle use signals increased work of breathing.
Purulent sputum is expected with pneumonia that is being treated.
Correct. An SpO₂ of 88% is below the prescribed target of 92% or higher and shows worsening gas exchange.
questions.rationale: The nurse must separate cues of acute deterioration from findings expected with a known diagnosis. Restlessness, speaking in 3–4 word phrases, accessory muscle use, and an SpO₂ below the prescribed target are cues of worsening gas exchange and increasing work of breathing. Purulent sputum and mild cough-related soreness are expected with treated pneumonia, and the midline trachea, symmetric expansion, orientation, and urine output are reassuring.
questions.takeaway: Restless, short phrases, accessory muscles, and falling SpO₂ = deterioration, not "just pneumonia."
questions.hintContent: Some findings are expected with treated pneumonia; others show that the work of breathing and gas exchange are getting worse.
questions.hintStrategy: For each finding, ask whether it is new and signals a change in oxygenation or breathing effort.

tabs.html: M.L., 30-year-old female. Persistent asthma since childhood. Admitted 3 days ago with a severe asthma exacerbation; required intubation for 20 hours. questions.stem: The nurse is analyzing M.L.’s 0300 assessment. Refer to the Nurses’ Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which finding is explained by both the asthma exacerbation and the pneumonia?
options: Expiratory wheezes in all lung fields
PaO₂ 58 mm Hg with SpO₂ 88% on 2 L/min
Crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lobe
Temperature 38.6 °C (101.5 °F)
optionRationales: Diffuse expiratory wheezes are an airway (bronchospasm) finding of asthma.
Correct. Narrowed airways and consolidated alveoli both create ventilation–perfusion mismatch, so both conditions cause hypoxemia.
Localized crackles with bronchial breath sounds reflect consolidation from pneumonia.
Fever reflects the infection (pneumonia), not bronchospasm.
questions.rationale: M.L. has two interacting problems. Diffuse wheezes and a prolonged expiratory phase are airway (bronchospasm) findings of asthma. Fever and localized crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the RLL are signs of consolidation from pneumonia. Hypoxemia results from both: narrowed airways and consolidated alveoli each create ventilation–perfusion mismatch.
questions.takeaway: Wheezes = asthma airways; localized crackles and fever = pneumonia; hypoxemia = both.
questions.hintContent: Think about the mechanism of each condition: one narrows the airways, the other fills alveoli. What outcome do they share?
questions.hintStrategy: Assign each finding to the condition that causes it; the correct answer is the one you cannot assign to only one.

tabs.html: M.L., 30-year-old female. Persistent asthma since childhood. Admitted 3 days ago with a severe asthma exacerbation; required intubation for 20 hours. questions.stem: The nurse compares M.L.’s 0315 arterial blood gas with the previous results. Refer to the Laboratory Results and Vital Signs. Which finding indicates the most immediate threat to M.L.?
options: Heart rate of 124/min with a temperature of 38.6 °C
WBC that rose to 15,800/mm³ while receiving IV corticosteroids
PaCO₂ that rose from 32 to 47 mm Hg while RR rose to 32/min
Right-sided chest soreness rated 2/10 with coughing
optionRationales: Tachycardia with fever fits the known pneumonia but is not the most immediate threat.
The WBC rise fits pneumonia and can also result from corticosteroids; it does not signal immediate danger.
Correct. A rising PaCO₂ despite rapid breathing means the respiratory muscles are tiring — a warning sign of impending respiratory failure.
Mild cough-related chest soreness is expected with pneumonia.
questions.rationale: Early in an asthma attack, the client hyperventilates and PaCO₂ is low (7.46/32). A "normal" or rising PaCO₂ in a client who is still breathing 32 times a minute means the respiratory muscles are tiring and ventilation is no longer adequate — a warning sign of impending acute respiratory failure. Tachycardia, fever, WBC, and chest soreness fit the known pneumonia but do not signal the most immediate threat.
questions.takeaway: In an asthma attack, a rising PaCO₂ in a fast-breathing client means fatigue and impending respiratory failure.
questions.hintContent: During an asthma attack, a client who is breathing fast should be blowing off CO₂. What does a rising CO₂ tell you?
questions.hintStrategy: Apply the ABCs: pick the finding that shows breathing is failing, over findings that fit the known infection.

tabs.html: M.L., 30-year-old female. Persistent asthma since childhood. Admitted 3 days ago with a severe asthma exacerbation; required intubation for 20 hours. Chest x-ray on admission: right lower lobe (RLL) infiltrate — community-acquired pneumonia. Extubated on hospital day 2 and transferred to the medical unit yesterday. No tobacco use. questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for M.L. at 0305. Refer to the Orders and Nurses' Notes. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care at this time? Select all that apply.
options: Administer the PRN albuterol nebulizer treatment
Increase the oxygen flow rate to reach the prescribed SpO₂ goal
Raise the head of the bed to high-Fowler's position
Administer lorazepam 0.5 mg IV for restlessness
Notify the provider of the assessment and ABG findings using SBAR
Hold the methylprednisolone dose because the client is febrile
optionRationales: Correct — a short-acting beta₂-agonist is the first-line reliever for acute bronchospasm; the PRN order covers this.
Correct — the order allows titration to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92%; the current 88% is below goal.
Correct — upright positioning lowers the diaphragm and improves lung expansion.
Incorrect — her restlessness is a sign of hypoxia; a benzodiazepine can depress the respiratory drive of a tiring client.
Correct — worsening hypoxemia and a rising PaCO₂ must be communicated promptly with a clear SBAR report.
Incorrect — systemic corticosteroids are essential to reduce airway inflammation; fever from treated pneumonia is not a reason to hold them without an order.
questions.rationale: The plan targets bronchospasm (SABA), hypoxemia (titrate oxygen, upright position), and escalation (SBAR to the provider). Sedating a hypoxic, tiring client and holding anti-inflammatory therapy are unsafe, and supine positioning worsens ventilation.
questions.takeaway: For a tiring asthmatic: bronchodilate, oxygenate, sit up, and escalate — never sedate.
questions.hintContent: Review which orders treat bronchospasm, which treat hypoxemia, and which drugs depress respiratory drive.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option on its own: does it improve airway, breathing, or oxygenation right now, or could it harm a client whose ventilation is already failing?

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
0300: Restless, speaking 3–4 words at a time, accessory muscle use, diffuse expiratory wheezes, RLL crackles. SpO₂ 88% on 2 L/min.

0310: Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized given. Oxygen increased to 4 L/min. Head of bed raised to high-Fowler's. Provider notified.

0340: Client now drowsy and closes eyes during questioning; arouses to voice. Breath sounds markedly diminished bilaterally with only faint wheezing. Shallow respirations. Skin diaphoretic; lips dusky.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Oxygen by nasal cannula; titrate to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92%
  • Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized every 4 hours and every 1 hour PRN wheezing/dyspnea
  • Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized every 6 hours
  • Methylprednisolone 40 mg IV every 12 hours
  • Ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours; azithromycin 500 mg IV every 24 hours
  • Lorazepam 0.5 mg IV every 6 hours PRN anxiety
  • ABG PRN respiratory distress; notify provider for SpO₂ < 90%

questions.stem: The nurse reassesses M.L. at 0340. Refer to the updated Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Allow the client to rest because the slower respirations and quieter wheezing show the nebulizer was effective
Obtain a repeat arterial blood gas and wait for the results before calling for assistance
Activate the rapid response team and stay with the client
Administer the next dose of methylprednisolone early to reduce airway inflammation
optionRationales: Incorrect — a 'quiet chest' with diminished breath sounds, drowsiness, and falling RR signals exhaustion and minimal airflow, not improvement.
Incorrect — delaying help to obtain data wastes time; the clinical picture already indicates respiratory failure.
Correct — drowsiness, shallow RR of 14, diminished breath sounds, and SpO₂ 84% on 6 L/min indicate impending respiratory arrest; the client needs immediate advanced airway support.
Incorrect — corticosteroids take hours to work, and giving a dose early requires an order; they will not reverse imminent arrest.
questions.rationale: A decreasing respiratory rate with decreased wheezing and falling level of consciousness in a client with severe asthma is a sign of respiratory muscle fatigue and CO₂ narcosis, not improvement. The priority is to summon the rapid response team (and prepare to assist ventilation with a bag-valve mask) while remaining with the client. Waiting for an ABG or giving slow-acting drugs delays life-saving care.
questions.takeaway: A 'silent chest' in asthma is an emergency — call for help, don't celebrate.
questions.hintContent: Recall why wheezing may fade and respiratory rate may fall as a severe asthma attack WORSENS.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare the 0340 data with 0300. The word 'first' plus a declining level of consciousness means choose the action that brings the most help the fastest.

tabs.title: Progress Note
tabs.html: Hospital day 9, 0900: After the rapid response on day 3, M.L. was transferred to the ICU for closer monitoring and returned to the medical unit on day 5. Blood cultures and sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to ceftriaxone; she is completing a 10-day course of IV antibiotics. Methylprednisolone changed to prednisone 40 mg PO daily. Discharge planned for day 10 if stable.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Day 9, 0800: Awake, alert, speaking in full sentences. Ambulated 150 ft in the hallway on room air. Faint expiratory wheezes. States she needed to sleep propped on 3 pillows last night because she "couldn't breathe lying down." Used the PRN albuterol nebulizer 4 times overnight for wheezing.

questions.stem: M.L. is now on hospital day 9, with discharge planned for tomorrow. Refer to the Progress Note, Nurses’ Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?
options: Speaking in full sentences and walking 150 ft on room air without distress
Temperature 37.1 °C (98.8 °F) and WBC 9,200/mm³
SpO₂ 93%–95% on room air
Used the PRN albuterol nebulizer 4 times overnight for wheezing
optionRationales: Full sentences and activity tolerance on room air show improvement.
A normal temperature and WBC show the infection is responding to antibiotics.
Maintaining SpO₂ on room air meets the oxygenation outcome.
Correct. Frequent rescue treatments show the airways are not controlled — the same warning sign that preceded her earlier collapse.
questions.rationale: Several outcome criteria are met: M.L. speaks in full sentences, tolerates activity, maintains her SpO₂ on room air, and is afebrile with a normal WBC as she completes IV antibiotics. However, repeated rescue treatments overnight (along with the new orthopnea) were the same warning signs that came before her collapse. They show her airways are not yet controlled and must be reported before discharge.
questions.takeaway: Increasing rescue-inhaler use = poor asthma control — report it before discharge.
questions.hintContent: Look for a finding that repeats the warning signs M.L. had before her earlier deterioration.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate findings that meet expected outcomes; the remaining one shows treatment is not yet effective.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
1410: 34-year-old client admitted 6 hours ago after a motor vehicle crash with right rib fractures (ribs 5–7) and a right pneumothorax. Right chest tube to –20 cm H₂O dry suction placed in the ED. Returned from CT scan at 1400; transport staff placed a clamp on the chest tube 'for safety' during transfer.

1425: Client reports sudden, severe shortness of breath and says 'something is wrong.' Anxious and diaphoretic. Trachea deviated to the left. Absent breath sounds on the right. Neck veins distended. No tidaling or bubbling in the water seal chamber.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a right chest tube for a pneumothorax. Refer to the Nurses’ Notes and Vital Signs. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Milk and strip the chest tube toward the drainage unit
Remove the clamp from the chest tube
Raise the drainage unit to the level of the bed
Place the client in Trendelenburg position
optionRationales: Stripping creates dangerous negative pressure and is not indicated; the problem is the clamp.
Correct. The clamp trapped air in the pleural space, causing tension pneumothorax; removing it restores drainage. The nurse then calls the rapid response team.
The drainage unit must stay below chest level to prevent backflow.
Trendelenburg position worsens breathing by pushing the abdominal contents against the diaphragm.
questions.rationale: Clamping a chest tube that is draining air from a pneumothorax allows air to accumulate under pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum (tracheal deviation). This compresses the heart and great vessels, reducing venous return (JVD, hypotension). The nurse removes the clamp immediately and summons emergency help, preparing for emergency decompression if needed; progress is shown by a midline trachea, returning breath sounds, and improving blood pressure and heart rate.
questions.takeaway: Never clamp a chest tube for transport — tension pneumothorax follows. Unclamp first.
questions.hintContent: Look at what changed between 1300 and 1425 and what the transport staff did to the tube.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the condition, then choose the action that removes its cause immediately.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Emergency department, 1120: 74-year-old client with severe COPD (home O₂ 2 L/min) brought in by family for 3 days of increased dyspnea and cough with thick green sputum. Family reports the client 'has been sleepier than usual today.' Client is drowsy but arouses to voice, sitting in tripod position, pursed-lip breathing, using accessory muscles. Diffuse expiratory wheezes with diminished bases. Arrived on home O₂ at 2 L/min by nasal cannula.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses’ Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which actions should the nurse take for this client? Select all that apply.
options: Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min to raise SpO₂ to 100%
Titrate oxygen to a target SpO₂ of 88%–92%
Administer PRN morphine to relieve air hunger
Administer the prescribed albuterol and ipratropium nebulizer treatment
Monitor level of consciousness and repeat the ABG
Encourage the client to lie supine to rest the respiratory muscles
optionRationales: High-concentration oxygen can worsen CO₂ retention in a client who chronically retains CO₂.
Correct. Controlled oxygen to 88%–92% corrects hypoxemia without worsening hypercapnia.
Morphine depresses respiration and would worsen CO₂ retention.
Correct. Bronchodilators open the airways and improve ventilation.
Correct. Level of consciousness and repeat ABG pH and PaCO₂ show whether ventilation is improving.
Lying supine reduces diaphragm movement; an upright or tripod position eases breathing.
questions.rationale: The client has a COPD exacerbation (increased dyspnea, sputum volume and purulence) with acute CO₂ retention on top of chronic CO₂ retention: pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 72 mm Hg, and a compensatory HCO₃⁻. Increasing drowsiness reflects CO₂ narcosis. Care focuses on controlled oxygen titrated to 88%–92% and bronchodilators to open the airways, with corticosteroids and antibiotics as prescribed. Level of consciousness and repeat ABGs show whether ventilation is improving.
questions.takeaway: COPD with hypercapnia: controlled O₂ (88–92%), bronchodilators, and watch LOC and PaCO₂.
questions.hintContent: The ABG shows acute CO₂ retention on top of chronic retention, and the client is getting sleepier.
questions.hintStrategy: Reject any action that would further depress breathing or push SpO₂ higher than the target for a CO₂ retainer.

tabs.title: Medication Administration Record
tabs.html:

  • Enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily
  • Incentive spirometer 10 times per hour while awake

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 67-year-old client on postoperative day 2 after an open colon resection. The client states, "It hurts too much to cough, so I just clear my throat." Refer to the Vital Signs and Medication Administration Record. Which findings indicate ineffective airway clearance? Select all that apply.
options: Pedal pulses 2+ bilaterally
Incentive spirometer volume 500 mL; preoperative goal 1,500 mL
Diminished breath sounds with fine crackles in both bases that do not clear with coughing
Abdominal incision edges approximated without drainage
Bowel sounds hypoactive in all 4 quadrants
Oral mucosa dry; drank 240 mL since 0000
optionRationales: Normal pedal pulses reflect peripheral circulation, not airway clearance.
Correct. Low incentive spirometer volumes show shallow, pain-limited breathing.
Correct. Basilar crackles that persist after coughing indicate retained secretions and early atelectasis.
An approximated incision is an expected healing finding.
Hypoactive bowel sounds are common after bowel surgery and do not reflect airway clearance.
Correct. Poor fluid intake thickens secretions and makes them harder to clear.
questions.rationale: Pain-limited coughing, low incentive spirometer volumes, and bibasilar crackles that do not clear with coughing are the defining cues of ineffective airway clearance and early atelectasis — reinforced by a new low-grade fever, tachypnea, and SpO₂ drop in the exhibit. Poor fluid intake thickens secretions. The nurse should medicate for pain, teach splinted coughing, raise the head of the bed, encourage fluids, and ambulate the client.
questions.takeaway: Pain-limited cough + low IS volumes + crackles that don’t clear = ineffective airway clearance.
questions.hintContent: Airway clearance depends on deep breaths, an effective cough, and thin secretions.
questions.hintStrategy: Select findings that affect breathing depth, cough effectiveness, or secretion thickness; ignore findings about other body systems.

tabs.title: Medication Administration Record
tabs.html:

  • Methylprednisolone 60 mg IV every 6 hours
  • Fluticasone 110 mcg MDI 2 puffs twice daily

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 52-year-old client admitted 12 hours ago with an asthma exacerbation. Refer to the Medication Administration Record and Laboratory Results. Which finding requires immediate follow-up with the provider?
options: New palpitations with an irregular apical pulse
Mild hand tremor and feeling jittery when holding a cup
Heart rate 104/min
Voice slightly hoarse
optionRationales: Correct. Irregular palpitations with a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L suggest dysrhythmias from hypokalemia and need prompt follow-up.
Tremor is an expected adverse effect of albuterol.
Mild tachycardia is an expected effect of frequent albuterol.
Hoarseness is a known effect of inhaled corticosteroids; it is not urgent.
questions.rationale: High-dose beta₂-agonists drive potassium into cells, and systemic corticosteroids increase renal potassium loss, so hypokalemia is a real risk; new irregular palpitations and muscle weakness with K⁺ 3.0 need prompt follow-up (cardiac monitoring, replacement). Systemic corticosteroids also cause hyperglycemia. Tremor, jitteriness, and mild tachycardia are expected albuterol effects.
questions.takeaway: Frequent albuterol + IV steroids → watch potassium; new irregular pulse is urgent.
questions.hintContent: Look at the potassium level and think about how albuterol and corticosteroids each affect it.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate expected adverse effects from a finding that could become life-threatening.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 70-year-old client admitted with pneumonia who has thick, tenacious sputum that is difficult to expectorate. The client has no history of heart or kidney failure. Which interventions should the nurse include to promote airway clearance? Select all that apply.
options: Encourage oral fluid intake of 2–3 L/day
Assist the client to ambulate in the hallway three times daily
Administer a cough suppressant every 4 hours around the clock
Provide humidified oxygen as prescribed
Keep the client supine to conserve energy
Offer an antihistamine at bedtime to dry secretions
optionRationales: Correct — adequate hydration thins secretions so they are easier to cough up.
Correct — mobility increases lung expansion and mobilizes secretions.
Incorrect — suppressing a productive cough causes retention of secretions.
Correct — humidification prevents drying of the airway mucosa and thickening of mucus.
Incorrect — immobility and supine positioning promote pooling of secretions and atelectasis.
Incorrect — antihistamines thicken secretions and make them harder to clear.
questions.rationale: Airway clearance improves when secretions are thinned (fluids, humidification) and mobilized (ambulation, position changes, effective coughing). Suppressing a productive cough, drying secretions with antihistamines, and immobility all promote mucus retention.
questions.takeaway: Thin it (fluids, humidity), move it (ambulate, turn), and cough it out — don't suppress it.
questions.hintContent: Think about the two goals of airway-clearance care: make secretions thinner and help move them out of the lungs.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option independently: does it thin or mobilize secretions, or does it thicken or trap them?

questions.stem: M.L.'s mother is learning to perform percussion, vibration, and postural drainage (PVD) at home for M.L.'s persistent congestion. Which statement by the mother indicates correct understanding?
options: "I'll clap with a flat palm directly over her spine, where it's easiest to reach."
"I'll clap with a cupped hand over her ribs, then vibrate while she breathes out."
"I'll give the acetylcysteine after the PVD so it can thin whatever is left."
"I'll do the treatments about 30 minutes after she finishes each meal."
optionRationales: A flat palm is less effective and uncomfortable, and percussion over the spine can cause injury; percuss over the ribs only.
Correct. A cupped hand over the ribs creates the air cushion that loosens mucus, and vibration during exhalation moves it toward the larger airways.
Nebulized treatments (albuterol, then acetylcysteine) are given before PVD so secretions are thinned and airways open when drainage begins.
Treatments soon after meals increase the risk of vomiting and aspiration; schedule PVD before meals.
questions.rationale: PVD loosens secretions and uses gravity to drain them toward the large airways so they can be coughed out. Percussion is done with a cupped hand over the ribs covering the congested area (never over the spine, sternum, or below the ribs), and vibration is applied during exhalation. Treatments are done before meals to prevent vomiting and aspiration, after the nebulized bronchodilator and mucolytic, and are followed by coughing.
questions.takeaway: PVD: cupped hand over the ribs, vibrate on exhalation, before meals, after the nebulizer — then cough.
questions.hintContent: Think about hand position, where on the chest percussion is safe, and when PVD should be timed around meals and medications.
questions.hintStrategy: This item asks for the CORRECT statement. Check each option for safe location, correct timing, and correct sequence.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: At a follow-up visit, a client with persistent asthma says, "I only use my fluticasone/salmeterol inhaler every few days because the copay is $85 a month, and I also have to buy albuterol." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Using it every few days is fine as long as your albuterol inhaler keeps working for you."
"Let's ask your provider and pharmacist about lower-cost options and assistance programs."
"You can use your albuterol every 4 hours instead so you don't need the controller."
"Your controller is the most important one, so you can stop buying the albuterol inhaler."
optionRationales: LABA + ICS combinations control chronic inflammation and bronchoconstriction only when taken every day as prescribed; skipping doses leads to exacerbations.
Correct. The nurse addresses the cost barrier directly and refers the client to resources, such as manufacturer assistance programs, that make daily adherence possible.
A short-acting rescue inhaler does not treat airway inflammation; relying on it signals poor control and raises the risk of a severe exacerbation.
The client still needs a rescue inhaler for sudden symptoms; stopping it is unsafe.
questions.rationale: Medication adherence is critical in chronic respiratory disease, and cost is a common barrier — clients often take several medications with high copays. Pharmaceutical companies may have programs to help with costs, and the provider or pharmacist may suggest less expensive options. The nurse identifies the barrier and connects the client with resources rather than accepting unsafe use of the controller or the rescue inhaler.
questions.takeaway: Cost is a major barrier to adherence — ask about it and connect clients with assistance programs.
questions.hintContent: The module lists expense, multiple medications, and higher copays as obstacles to adherence, along with one resource that may help.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the response that removes the barrier while keeping both the controller and the rescue medication safe.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse observes a client with COPD demonstrating the use of a new fluticasone/salmeterol dry powder inhaler (disk device). Which action by the client requires the nurse to intervene?
options: Holds the device level after sliding the lever to load the dose
Exhales fully into the mouthpiece before inhaling the dose
Inhales quickly and deeply through the mouthpiece
Rinses the mouth with water and spits after the dose
optionRationales: Incorrect — keeping the device level after loading prevents loss of the powder; this is correct technique.
Correct — exhaling into a dry powder inhaler blows moisture into it and can disperse the powder, so the client receives an incomplete dose; exhale away from the device.
Incorrect — DPIs require a quick, forceful, deep inhalation to draw the powder into the lungs.
Incorrect — rinsing and spitting after an inhaled corticosteroid reduces the risk of oral candidiasis and hoarseness.
questions.rationale: Dry powder inhalers are breath-activated and require a rapid, deep inhalation. They are not shaken and are not used with a spacer. The client should exhale away from the mouthpiece, because moisture from breath clumps the powder and blows the dose out. After an ICS-containing inhaler, the client rinses and spits.
questions.takeaway: DPI: exhale away, seal lips, breathe in fast and deep, rinse and spit.
questions.hintContent: Recall how a dry powder inhaler delivers medication differently from a pressurized MDI.
questions.hintStrategy: The item asks which action needs INTERVENTION — look for the one incorrect step among correct steps.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with allergic asthma receives a scheduled allergen immunotherapy (allergy shot) injection in the clinic. Ten minutes later, the client reports throat tightness and itching. The nurse notes hives on the chest, audible wheezing, HR 118/min, and BP 86/50 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Administer an oral antihistamine and observe for 30 minutes
Administer the client's albuterol inhaler 2 puffs
Apply ice to the injection site to slow absorption
Administer epinephrine intramuscularly per protocol
optionRationales: Incorrect — antihistamines relieve hives but do not reverse airway edema or hypotension; they are adjuncts only.
Incorrect — albuterol may help wheezing but does not treat the systemic reaction or hypotension.
Incorrect — local measures do not treat systemic anaphylaxis.
Correct — hives with airway symptoms and hypotension after allergen exposure is anaphylaxis; IM epinephrine is the first-line, life-saving treatment.
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis is a known risk of allergen immunotherapy, which is why clients are observed for at least 30 minutes after each injection in a setting with emergency equipment. Multisystem signs (skin, airway, hypotension) require immediate IM epinephrine, which reverses bronchoconstriction, laryngeal edema, and vasodilation. Antihistamines, bronchodilators, oxygen, and fluids are adjuncts.
questions.takeaway: Anaphylaxis = epinephrine IM first; everything else is second.
questions.hintContent: Recall the first-line drug for anaphylaxis and why adjunct drugs are not enough.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the condition from the cluster of cues, then select the single action that reverses the most life-threatening problems at once.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the home medications of a 25-year-old client with asthma who says, "I get confused about which one to use when I’m wheezing." Which medications should the nurse teach the client to use for quick relief of wheezing? Select all that apply.
options: Albuterol MDI
Fluticasone MDI
Theophylline extended-release tablet
Salmeterol/fluticasone DPI
Albuterol nebulizer solution
optionRationales: Correct. Albuterol is a short-acting beta-agonist that relieves bronchospasm within minutes.
Inhaled corticosteroids reduce inflammation over days to weeks and are long-term control medications.
Extended-release theophylline is taken on a schedule to maintain bronchodilation, not for rescue.
A LABA + ICS combination is used for long-term control, not acute relief.
Correct. Nebulized albuterol is also a short-acting rescue bronchodilator.
questions.rationale: Short-acting beta-agonists (SABAs) such as albuterol, by inhaler or nebulizer, relieve bronchospasm within minutes and are the rescue medications. Inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation over days to weeks, LABA + ICS combinations are used for chronic control, and xanthines such as theophylline are taken on a schedule to maintain bronchodilation. Controllers are taken every day, even when the client feels well.
questions.takeaway: Rescue = short-acting albuterol (any device); everything else is a daily controller.
questions.hintContent: A quick-relief medication must work within minutes; controllers reduce inflammation or maintain bronchodilation over time.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the drug class of each medication, regardless of the delivery device.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: An 81-year-old client with COPD and arthritis in both hands is prescribed an albuterol metered-dose inhaler. During a return demonstration, the client sprays the dose, then inhales 2 seconds later, and a visible mist escapes from the mouth. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Teach the client to hold the inhaler 2 inches from the open mouth
Request a prescription for a spacer (valved holding chamber)
Tell the client to take 4 puffs instead of 2 to compensate
Suggest the client inhale the dose through the nose
optionRationales: Incorrect — the open-mouth technique still requires precise coordination, which this client lacks.
Correct — a spacer holds the medication so the client does not need to coordinate actuation and inhalation, improving lung deposition.
Incorrect — increasing the dose without a prescription is unsafe and does not fix the technique.
Incorrect — inhalers are designed for oral inhalation to reach the lower airways.
questions.rationale: Older adults often have difficulty coordinating MDI actuation with inhalation because of arthritis, weakness, or cognitive changes. A spacer or valved holding chamber allows the client to press the canister and then inhale slowly, increasing the dose reaching the lungs and reducing oropharyngeal deposition.
questions.takeaway: Poor hand–breath coordination with an MDI? Add a spacer.
questions.hintContent: Recall the purpose of a spacer and the coordination skill an MDI requires.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the specific technique error in the stem and choose the option that removes that problem.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client had a chest tube inserted 2 days ago for a spontaneous pneumothorax. On the previous shift, the water seal chamber showed intermittent bubbling with exhalation. Now the nurse notes continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber. The client's respirations are 18/min and unlabored, and SpO₂ is 96%. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Check the dressing and all tubing connections for a leak
Clamp the chest tube near the insertion site and leave it clamped for 1 hour
Document the finding as expected during lung re-expansion
Increase the suction level to remove the air more quickly
optionRationales: Correct — a new continuous air leak often comes from a loose connection or dislodged tube; the nurse checks the dressing and all connections first.
Incorrect — prolonged clamping without an order can cause tension pneumothorax.
Incorrect — continuous bubbling is not expected; intermittent bubbling with exhalation or coughing is.
Incorrect — changing suction requires an order and does not locate the leak.
questions.rationale: Intermittent bubbling with exhalation or cough means air is still leaving the pleural space. A change to continuous bubbling suggests a system leak (loose connection, crack, tube pulled back with an eyelet outside the chest). Because the client is stable, the nurse inspects the insertion site and connections first; if the leak cannot be found, the provider is notified.
questions.takeaway: New continuous bubbling in the water seal = check for a leak, starting at the client and working toward the unit.
questions.hintContent: Recall what intermittent versus continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber indicates.
questions.hintStrategy: The client is stable, so gather data about the equipment before making changes. Eliminate options that are unsafe or require an order.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to assist the provider with removing a client's chest tube. Which actions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Administer the prescribed analgesic about 30 minutes before removal
Instruct the client to breathe in and out deeply while the tube is pulled
Teach the client to take a deep breath and hold it (or bear down) as the tube is removed
Have an airtight petrolatum gauze dressing ready to cover the site immediately
Clamp the chest tube for 24 hours before removal as a routine step
Monitor for dyspnea and decreased SpO₂ after removal
optionRationales: Correct — chest tube removal is painful; premedication improves comfort and cooperation.
Incorrect — inhaling while the tube is withdrawn can draw air into the pleural space.
Correct — breath-holding or a Valsalva maneuver keeps intrathoracic pressure positive and prevents air entry.
Correct — an occlusive dressing seals the site to prevent air from entering.
Incorrect — clamping is done only if specifically prescribed (e.g., a clamp trial), not routinely.
Correct — recurrent pneumothorax can occur; a follow-up chest x-ray is usually ordered.
questions.rationale: Safe chest tube removal involves premedication, having the client hold the breath or perform a Valsalva maneuver during removal, immediately sealing the site with an occlusive dressing, and monitoring for recurrence of pneumothorax (dyspnea, decreased breath sounds, falling SpO₂) with a follow-up x-ray.
questions.takeaway: Chest tube out: premedicate, breath-hold, seal the site, and watch for recurrence.
questions.hintContent: Recall how intrathoracic pressure changes during inspiration and why that matters when an opening is created in the chest wall.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option ask: would this let air into the pleural space or prevent it? Judge each option independently.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with emphysema calls the nurse after a coughing spell, reporting sudden sharp left-sided chest pain that worsens with breathing. The nurse finds diminished breath sounds and decreased chest wall movement on the left, RR 30/min, and SpO₂ 86% on 2 L/min. Which explanation of these findings is most accurate?
options: Fluid shifted from the capillaries into the alveoli, causing acute pulmonary edema
A blood clot lodged in a pulmonary artery branch, blocking blood flow to the lung
A bulla ruptured, letting air into the pleural space and collapsing the lung
Fluid accumulated in the pleural space from inflammation, causing an effusion
optionRationales: Pulmonary edema causes bilateral crackles, not sudden one-sided pleuritic pain with decreased chest movement.
A pulmonary embolism does not cause unilateral absent breath sounds and decreased chest wall movement.
Correct. Emphysema creates bullae that can rupture with coughing, causing a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax and loss of negative intrapleural pressure.
A pleural effusion develops gradually rather than suddenly after a coughing spell.
questions.rationale: Clients with emphysema have enlarged, weakened air spaces (bullae/blebs) that can rupture, especially with coughing, allowing air into the pleural space. This is a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax. The normally negative intrapleural pressure that holds the lung against the chest wall is lost, and the lung collapses, causing sudden pleuritic pain, decreased breath sounds, and asymmetric chest movement on the affected side.
questions.takeaway: Emphysema + coughing + sudden one-sided pleuritic pain = think ruptured bulla (pneumothorax).
questions.hintContent: Consider what emphysema does to the structure of the air spaces and what a forceful cough could do to them.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the onset (sudden) and the one-sided findings to the mechanism that fits both.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 79-year-old client who had a stroke 3 days ago and has mild dysphagia. The client is at risk for aspiration pneumonia. Which interventions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the head of the bed elevated at least 30° at all times unless contraindicated
Ensure a swallow screen is completed before giving oral food, fluids, or medications
Provide oral care at least twice daily
Encourage the client to drink thin liquids through a straw
Have the client sit upright with the chin tucked while swallowing
Place the client flat for 30 minutes after meals to aid digestion
optionRationales: Correct — head-of-bed elevation reduces reflux and aspiration.
Correct — a swallow screen identifies dysphagia before anything is given by mouth.
Correct — oral care reduces the bacterial load that can be aspirated into the lungs.
Incorrect — straws and thin liquids increase the speed and volume of fluid reaching the pharynx, raising aspiration risk in dysphagia.
Correct — upright positioning with a chin tuck helps protect the airway during swallowing.
Incorrect — the client should remain upright for at least 30 minutes after eating.
questions.rationale: Older adults and clients after a stroke have diminished cough and gag reflexes and increased risk of aspiration pneumonia. Evidence-based prevention includes swallow screening, upright positioning with a chin tuck, head-of-bed elevation, oral hygiene, and avoiding thin liquids through straws unless cleared by speech-language pathology.
questions.takeaway: Prevent aspiration: screen the swallow, sit up, tuck the chin, clean the mouth, skip the straw.
questions.hintContent: Recall how aging and stroke affect cough, gag, and swallow reflexes, and what reduces the volume of oral bacteria aspirated.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each option as true/false: does it protect the airway during and after eating, or does it increase the chance of material entering the trachea?

tabs.title: Admission Orders
tabs.html:
• Chest x-ray — completed, shows left lower lobe infiltrate
  • Blood cultures ×2 sets
  • Sputum culture and Gram stain
  • Ceftriaxone 1 g IV now, then every 24 hours
  • Azithromycin 500 mg IV daily
  • Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN temperature > 38.3 °C (101 °F)

questions.stem: A client is admitted with suspected community-acquired pneumonia. Refer to the Admission Orders and Vital Signs. Which order should the nurse implement first?
options: Administer acetaminophen 650 mg PO
Administer ceftriaxone 1 g IV
Obtain blood cultures
Administer azithromycin 500 mg IV
optionRationales: Incorrect — fever reduction improves comfort but does not take priority over time-sensitive culture collection before antibiotics.
Incorrect — antibiotics should be started promptly, but cultures must be drawn first so the antibiotic does not interfere with organism growth.
Correct — obtaining cultures before the first antibiotic dose allows accurate identification of the organism; antibiotics should follow without delay.
Incorrect — like ceftriaxone, it should be given after cultures are obtained.
questions.rationale: Blood and sputum cultures should be obtained before the first antibiotic dose because antibiotics can sterilize cultures and prevent identification of the pathogen and its sensitivities. Cultures must not delay antibiotic therapy — the nurse obtains them quickly and then administers antibiotics promptly.
questions.takeaway: Cultures before antibiotics — then give the antibiotics without delay.
questions.hintContent: Recall why the timing of specimen collection relative to antibiotics matters for culture results.
questions.hintStrategy: All orders are appropriate; determine which one becomes impossible to do correctly if done later.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with COPD who already uses pursed-lip breathing reports becoming very short of breath while climbing stairs at home. The nurse teaches diaphragmatic (abdominal) breathing. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Place one hand on your abdomen and one on your chest.
Inhale slowly through your nose so your abdomen rises while your chest stays still.
Raise your shoulders as you inhale to open your chest.
Hold your breath for 30 seconds before you exhale.
Exhale slowly while gently tightening your abdominal muscles.
Force the air out as hard as you can with each breath.
optionRationales: Correct. Hand placement lets the client feel whether the abdomen or chest is moving.
Correct. The abdomen should rise as the diaphragm descends, with little chest movement.
Raising the shoulders uses accessory muscles and increases the work of breathing.
Prolonged breath-holding worsens air trapping and dyspnea.
Correct. Gently contracting the abdominal muscles moves the diaphragm up during exhalation.
Forceful exhalation collapses small airways and worsens air trapping.
questions.rationale: Diaphragmatic breathing shifts the work of breathing to the diaphragm and away from the neck and shoulder accessory muscles, which lowers the work of breathing. The client places one hand on the abdomen and one on the chest, inhales slowly through the nose so the abdomen rises while the chest stays relatively still, and exhales slowly (often through pursed lips) while gently tightening the abdominal muscles to move the diaphragm up. Forceful exhalation and prolonged breath-holding worsen air trapping and dyspnea.
questions.takeaway: Diaphragmatic breathing: belly rises on a slow nose inhale, gentle abdominal squeeze on a slow exhale.
questions.hintContent: The goal is to let the diaphragm do the work and rest the neck and shoulder muscles.
questions.hintStrategy: Reject any instruction that uses accessory muscles or traps air in the lungs.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 19-year-old client with asthma has a personal best peak expiratory flow (PEF) of 400 L/min. The nurse reviews the client’s home log using the asthma action plan. Which entry required immediate action?
options: Monday: PEF 360 L/min, no symptoms
Tuesday: PEF 280 L/min, coughing and mild chest tightness
Friday: PEF 300 L/min, woke at night coughing
Wednesday: PEF 180 L/min, trouble walking and talking
optionRationales: 360 L/min is 90% of personal best with no symptoms — green zone.
280 L/min is 70% of personal best with mild symptoms — yellow zone: add quick-relief medication and monitor.
300 L/min is 75% of personal best with nighttime cough — yellow zone.
Correct. 180 L/min is 45% of personal best with trouble walking and talking — red zone: take rescue medication and get emergency care.
questions.rationale: Asthma action plan zones are based on percentage of personal best PEF and symptoms: green ≥ 80% (continue controller), yellow 50%–79% (caution: add quick-relief medication, contact provider if not improving), red < 50% (medical alert: rescue medication and emergency care).
questions.takeaway: Red zone (< 50% of personal best or trouble walking/talking) = rescue medication and emergency care now.
questions.hintContent: Calculate each PEF as a percentage of the personal best of 400 L/min.
questions.hintStrategy: Green ≥ 80%, yellow 50%–79%, red < 50%; the red-zone entry demands immediate action.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client at 32 weeks' gestation is admitted with an asthma exacerbation. She is wheezing, RR 26/min, SpO₂ 93% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula, and the fetal heart rate is within the expected range. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Position the client supine with the head of the bed flat so that she can rest
Check each prescribed medication for safety in pregnancy before giving it
Notify the obstetric provider only after the asthma is controlled
Hold the oxygen because the SpO₂ is above 90%
optionRationales: Incorrect — prolonged supine positioning can harm the fetus, and lying flat worsens dyspnea; an upright or side-tilted position is preferred.
Correct — the nurse checks all medications before administering them to a pregnant client.
Incorrect — treatment should involve both the pulmonologist and the obstetrician from the start, not after the exacerbation resolves.
Incorrect — oxygenation must be maintained for both mother and fetus; oxygen is continued as prescribed and the client monitored.
questions.rationale: The fetus depends on maternal oxygenation, so the underlying condition must be resolved promptly to keep oxygen levels adequate for both mother and fetus. The module directs the nurse to check all medications before administering them, to involve both the pulmonologist and the obstetrician in treatment, to avoid positioning that may harm the fetus (prolonged supine), and to monitor oxygenation status.
questions.takeaway: Pregnancy + respiratory problem: check every medication, involve pulmonology and obstetrics, avoid prolonged supine, protect maternal oxygenation.
questions.hintContent: Recall the pregnancy points on the Lifespan Considerations slides: medications, positioning, and which providers should be involved.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that could reduce oxygen delivery to the fetus or delay collaboration; choose the safe medication practice.

tabs.title: Home Health Visit
tabs.html:
Baseline (last month): SpO₂ 91% on 2 L/min; uses albuterol about twice weekly; white sputum in the morning; walks to mailbox without stopping.

Today: SpO₂ 87% on 2 L/min; used albuterol 5 times since yesterday; sputum thick and green, more than usual; had to stop twice walking to the bathroom. Barrel-shaped chest, clubbed fingers, and pursed-lip breathing noted. T 37.8 °C (100 °F).

questions.stem: The home health nurse visits a 68-year-old client with COPD. Refer to the Home Health Visit note. Which findings indicate that the client may be experiencing an acute exacerbation of COPD? Select all that apply.
options: SpO₂ 87% on 2 L/min
Increased use of albuterol
Thick green sputum in greater amounts
Barrel-shaped chest
Pursed-lip breathing
Needing to stop while walking to the bathroom
optionRationales: Indicates exacerbation — SpO₂ is lower than the client's baseline of 91% on the same oxygen flow.
Indicates exacerbation — increased rescue medication use shows worsening symptoms.
Indicates exacerbation — increased sputum volume and purulence are cardinal signs of an exacerbation.
Chronic finding — barrel chest reflects long-standing hyperinflation.
Chronic finding — pursed-lip breathing is a learned compensatory technique.
Indicates exacerbation — decreased activity tolerance compared with baseline shows increased dyspnea.
questions.rationale: A COPD exacerbation is an acute worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond day-to-day variation — increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and increased sputum purulence — often with more rescue inhaler use and lower SpO₂ than baseline. Barrel chest, clubbing, and pursed-lip breathing are chronic findings that do not indicate an acute change.
questions.takeaway: COPD exacerbation = worse than THIS client's baseline: more dyspnea, more sputum, more purulent sputum.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three cardinal symptoms of a COPD exacerbation and which physical findings develop over years.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare 'Today' with 'Baseline.' Select only findings that CHANGED; chronic findings are present in both.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 22-year-old client arrives in the emergency department with an acute asthma exacerbation: speaking in phrases, RR 30/min, diffuse wheezes, SpO₂ 89% on room air. The provider prescribes oxygen, albuterol by nebulizer, and prednisone 50 mg PO. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Administer prednisone 50 mg PO
Position the client upright
Administer the albuterol nebulizer treatment
Reassess breath sounds and peak flow
optionRationales: Systemic corticosteroids reduce inflammation but take hours to work, so they follow oxygen and the bronchodilator.
Correct. Upright positioning is immediate, needs no equipment, and improves lung expansion and ventilation.
The bronchodilator is essential but follows positioning and oxygen application.
Reassessment evaluates the response after interventions are given.
questions.rationale: Upright positioning is immediate and improves ventilation. Oxygen then corrects hypoxemia. A short-acting beta-agonist relieves bronchospasm within minutes. Systemic corticosteroids reduce inflammation but act over hours, so they follow the bronchodilator. The nurse then reassesses the response to treatment.
questions.takeaway: Acute asthma: sit up → oxygen → albuterol → steroid → reassess.
questions.hintContent: Think about which intervention can be done instantly and improves breathing mechanics without waiting for equipment or drug effect.
questions.hintStrategy: Among correct actions, choose the fastest one that improves ventilation; slower-acting drugs come later.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Health Promotion & Smoking Cessation
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: During an annual visit, a 46-year-old client who smokes 1 pack per day says, 'My dad just had a heart attack. I want to quit within the next month, but I've failed before.' Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Help the client set a quit date and choose cessation aids
Explain the long-term health consequences of continued smoking in detail, including heart disease
Encourage the client to cut down gradually over the next year
Document the client's smoking status and revisit it at the next annual visit
optionRationales: Correct — the client is ready to quit; the nurse helps develop a plan with a quit date, discusses nicotine replacement, and provides a referral.
Incorrect — the client is already motivated; a detailed lecture does not give the help the client is asking for.
Incorrect — a year-long reduction without a quit plan is less effective than planned cessation with support.
Incorrect — delaying assistance misses a teachable moment.
questions.rationale: This client is ready to quit, so the nurse helps the client develop a plan with a quit date and provides a referral to counseling or a quitline. Nicotine replacement therapy (patch, gum, lozenge, oral inhaler, or nasal spray) combined with behavioral counseling increases the likelihood of abstinence, which is especially important for a client who has failed before.
questions.takeaway: Ready to quit? Assist: set a date, make a plan, add counseling and medication.
questions.hintContent: Recall what the module says the nurse should do when a client expresses interest in quitting.
questions.hintStrategy: Determine the client's stage of readiness from the stem first, then choose the action that matches that stage.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 55-year-old client with COPD asks how to prevent respiratory infections. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Receive an influenza vaccine every year
Ask your provider about the pneumococcal vaccine
Encourage people you live with to get a yearly influenza vaccine
Avoid vaccines, because COPD makes them unsafe
One influenza vaccine gives lifelong protection
optionRationales: Correct — influenza vaccination is repeated every year because the circulating viruses change.
Correct — pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for adults with chronic lung disease.
Correct — vaccinating household contacts decreases transmission to the client.
Incorrect — chronic lung disease is a reason to be vaccinated, not a reason to avoid vaccines.
Incorrect — influenza vaccine protection lasts about one season, so it is needed yearly.
questions.rationale: Infectious illnesses of the respiratory tract threaten oxygenation, and clients with chronic lung disease are at high risk for complications. Vaccination is encouraged to decrease transmission of preventable diseases. The influenza vaccine is given every year, the pneumococcal vaccine protects against a common cause of pneumonia, and vaccinating household members reduces the client's exposure.
questions.takeaway: COPD health promotion: yearly flu shot, pneumococcal vaccine, and vaccinated household contacts.
questions.hintContent: Recall why the module encourages vaccination and how often the influenza vaccine is given.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each statement for accuracy and whether it reduces the client's exposure to preventable respiratory infections.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Health Promotion & Smoking Cessation
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 4-year-old client with asthma who has had three ED visits this year. The parent says, 'I only smoke in the car with the windows down or outside, never around my child.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: 'That's a good plan. Smoking outside the home and away from your child completely protects your child's lungs.'
'Opening the car windows is enough to clear the smoke before your child rides.'
'Your child should use the rescue inhaler before riding in the car.'
'Smoke residue in the car and on clothes can still trigger asthma. Can we talk about quitting?'
optionRationales: Incorrect — smoke residue on clothing, hair, and surfaces (thirdhand smoke) still exposes the child.
Incorrect — car interiors retain smoke particles and residue even with windows open.
Incorrect — premedicating does not remove the trigger and normalizes ongoing exposure.
Correct — this corrects the misconception about exposure and opens a nonjudgmental conversation about cessation, the most effective protection.
questions.rationale: Children are more vulnerable to tobacco smoke because of smaller airways and higher respiratory rates. Secondhand and thirdhand smoke (residue on surfaces, clothing, and car interiors) are asthma triggers. The best protection is a smoke-free home and car and parental cessation; the nurse should address this respectfully and offer support.
questions.takeaway: No 'safe' place to smoke around an asthmatic child — residue travels on clothes and in cars.
questions.hintContent: Recall how tobacco smoke exposure affects children's airways and the concept of thirdhand smoke.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the response that both corrects the misconception and keeps communication therapeutic and nonjudgmental.

questions.ref: Module 15 · Oxygenation · Health Promotion & Smoking Cessation
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client with COPD how to reduce exposure to airborne irritants at home and in the community. Which client statements indicate a need for further teaching? Select all that apply.
options: "I’ll check the daily air quality index and stay indoors when it is poor."
"Using my wood-burning fireplace every evening will keep the air warm and dry for my lungs."
"I’ll use a HEPA air filter in my bedroom."
"I’ll spray aerosol air fresheners to cover odors that bother my breathing."
"I’ll ask my family not to smoke inside the house or car."
optionRationales: Monitoring the air quality index and staying indoors on poor days reduces exposure.
Correct. Wood smoke is an airborne irritant that triggers airway inflammation.
A HEPA filter reduces indoor airborne particles.
Correct. Aerosol sprays are chemical irritants that can trigger bronchospasm.
Avoiding secondhand smoke reduces exposure to a major irritant.
questions.rationale: Airborne irritants such as cigarette smoke, wood smoke, pollution, and chemical sprays trigger airway inflammation. Managing environmental air quality — monitoring the air quality index, filtering indoor air, and avoiding smoke and aerosols — reduces exposure and exacerbations.
questions.takeaway: Avoid smoke (tobacco or wood) and aerosols; filter the air and watch the air quality index.
questions.hintContent: The question asks for statements that show a misunderstanding — ones that would increase exposure to irritants.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old client has smoked 1½ packs of cigarettes per day for 20 years and says, "My lungs must be fine, because I don’t get short of breath." Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: "You have a 30 pack-year history; damage often shows only once it is irreversible."
"You have a 20 pack-year history, which is below the level linked with lung damage."
"Smoke mainly lowers surfactant production, so shortness of breath would appear early."
"Smoke speeds up cilia in the airways, so your lungs are clearing the damage as it happens."
optionRationales: Correct. 1.5 packs × 20 years = 30 pack-years; decline in lung function often becomes noticeable only after irreversible damage.
Pack-years = packs per day × years, so the history is 30 pack-years, and there is no safe threshold.
Tobacco smoke increases mucus production; symptoms often appear late, not early.
Tobacco smoke reduces cilia action, so secretions are not cleared well.
questions.rationale: Pack-years = packs per day × years smoked (1.5 × 20 = 30). Tobacco smoke increases mucus production and reduces cilia action in the airway passages, so secretions are not cleared well. With prolonged exposure, pulmonary function declines, but the decline often becomes noticeable only after irreversible damage has occurred — so feeling well does not mean the lungs are undamaged.
questions.takeaway: Pack-years = packs/day × years; no symptoms does not mean no damage.
questions.hintContent: Calculate pack-years first, then recall what smoke does to mucus and cilia.
questions.hintStrategy: Check both the math and the pathophysiology in each option; eliminate any option wrong on either.

questions.stem: A client who stopped smoking 4 days ago calls the clinic reporting irritability, trouble concentrating, increased appetite, and a cough that seems 'worse than when I smoked.' The client asks whether to start smoking again. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: 'These are expected withdrawal effects, and coughing often increases as your airways clear.'
'Your symptoms mean you quit too quickly; cutting back gradually over several months would work better.'
'These are signs of a respiratory infection, so you should come in today to be started on antibiotics.'
'A worsening cough after quitting usually means permanent lung damage has already occurred.'
optionRationales: Correct — nicotine withdrawal peaks in the first several days and fades over weeks; as cilia recover, the cough can temporarily increase to clear mucus.
Incorrect — abrupt quitting is effective; symptoms are expected and do not mean the approach failed.
Incorrect — without fever or purulent sputum, these findings fit withdrawal and recovery, not infection.
Incorrect — this is inaccurate and may discourage the client from continuing.
questions.rationale: Nicotine withdrawal symptoms (irritability, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, increased appetite, insomnia) peak within the first few days and subside over 2–4 weeks. Smoking paralyzes and damages cilia; as ciliary function returns, a temporary increase in cough helps clear accumulated mucus. The nurse reassures, reinforces the benefits, and suggests coping strategies or NRT.
questions.takeaway: A 'quitter's cough' is a sign of healing cilia, not failure.
questions.hintContent: Recall how smoking affects cilia and the typical timeline of nicotine withdrawal.
questions.hintStrategy: Interpret the symptoms in the context of the recent change (quitting), and choose the response that is accurate and supports continued abstinence.
